newsitem.title: USA: U.S. swap spreads creep wider, shorter end busy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. swap spreads creep wider, shorter end busy.

text.p: U.S. interest rate swap spreads were generally creeping wider this week, with the shorter end seeing good interest, traders said on Thursday.

"I think the market's been pretty busy," a bank trader in New York said of the activity in the three- to five-year market. "A lot of new (corporate debt) issues are coming in to the market, trying to take advantage of lower interest rates."

Despite mushrooming corporate debt issues, hedging for further future offerings and anticipation that Treasury supplies would continue to decline kept an upward pressure on longer-dated swaps, traders said.
Spreads in the 10-year area shrank briefly after the Treasury's announcement on Wednesday of next week's refunding schedule but has since bounced back, said a bank trader in the West Coast.
"It caused the spreads to come in slightly because the roll into the new issue is a give-up...although they seem to be coming back right now," he said.

The 10-year spread stood at around 40 basis points bid, 41 offered, half a point wider from last Friday. Two-year was assessed at 29 bps bid and 30 bps offered, with five-year at 31-1/4 versus 32, both about two points wider.

Traders said that overall, the refunding, which included a relatively small 30-year bond offering of $10 billion, added to the already prevailing perception that Treasury supplies would become increasingly tighter, they said.
"Going forward, it's just going to get expectations for lower and lower issuance," the New York trader said. "Hopefully it continues to go lower. Otherwise, there's going to be a massive whipsaw."
The Treasury is due to auction $16 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday, $12 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year notes on Thursday.
Traders said a bulk of recent longer-term corporate debt had probably not been swapped into floating rates.
Instead, the West Coast trader said, entities planning debt offerings in the next several months were trying to lock in at present rates by paying fixed via swaps at this point.
"Instead of being a receiver of fixed, they would be a payor of fixed," he said. "I think that's the dominant influence right now."
Among recent big issues were International Business Machines Corp's 500 million 10-year debt and another $500 million in 30-years launched on Wednesday.
The 10-year seen priced at 44 bps over Treasuries and the 30-year at 19 bps over.
With current benchmark 30-year T-bond yield at around 6.3 percent, those prices would be fairly comfortable fixed rate levels for issuers, traders said.
"I think some of them (recent debt issues) are definitely swaps-driven, but I don't know about those really long ones," the New York bank trader said.
Harcourt General Inc today launched $150 million in 10-year, $200 million in 30-year and 150 million in 100-year tranches.
